items.availability_note: NMN is genuinely present in plant and animal foods, but at sub-milligram-per-100 g levels, roughly 100 to 1,000 times below a single capsule. The reference dataset (Mills et al. 2016, Cell Metab, PMID 28068222 / DOI 10.1016/j.cmet.2016.09.013) puts every food it measured between 0 and 1.88 mg/100 g. A 2025 HPLC-DAD/LC-MS-MS survey of plant foods (Alegre & Pastore, CyTA J Food, DOI 10.1080/19476337.2025.2458753) found NMN spanning 40 to 13,000 ug/100 g, richest in broccoli and green beans, which is the same order of magnitude. Cow milk is not a meaningful NMN source: its NAD+ precursor content is dominated by nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside, not NMN (Trammell et al. 2016, PMID 27052539). Supplement NMN is not extracted from food, it is made by microbial fermentation or enzymatic/chemical synthesis.

items.dose_gap: Unbridgeable. Taking the richest food at its richest measured value (edamame, 1.88 mg/100 g), a 250 mg dose needs 13.3 kg of edamame a day, and at the low end of the same food's range (0.47 mg/100 g) it needs 53 kg. A 1,000 mg dose needs 53-213 kg. Broccoli: 250 mg requires 22-100 kg, about 245 to 1,100 cups. Avocado: 250 mg requires 104-463 whole avocados a day. Cucumber peel is the most quoted 'NMN food' and the least useful: you would have to pare the skin off roughly 1,250 cucumbers to reach 250 mg. There is no eating pattern that reaches a supplement dose, and no reason to think the trace dietary amounts do anything a supplement dose is claimed to do.
items.form_caveat: Substantial. NMN is a phosphorylated nucleotide and is not absorbed intact in any large quantity: it is dephosphorylated in the gut to nicotinamide riboside and then to nicotinamide before or during absorption, so an oral NMN capsule is partly a nicotinamide delivery system. Food NMN arrives as a minor component of a mixed NAD+ vitamer pool (nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, NR, NAD+ itself) inside intact cells and is measured after extraction, not necessarily released by chewing and digestion. Supplement material is manufactured by fermentation or enzymatic synthesis, never extracted from broccoli or edamame despite the marketing imagery. Regulatory status also differs: the FDA has taken the position that NMN is precluded from being marketed as a US dietary supplement, while it is sold freely elsewhere, so 'food-derived' framing on a label carries no compositional meaning.
items.bioavailability: Food NMN quantities are too small for bioavailability to matter. For the supplement form, human and mouse tracer work shows the oral route delivers NAD+ precursors largely after conversion to nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide rather than as intact NMN (Trammell et al. 2016, Nat Commun 7:12948, DOI 10.1038/ncomms12948, for the NR side of the same pathway). Separately, ordinary diets already supply 15-20 mg/day of niacin equivalents feeding the same NAD+ pathway, which is thousands of times more molar precursor than the NMN in any vegetable portion, so the scarcity premise behind NMN supplementation is not a dietary-shortfall argument.

items.availability_note: NR is a real dietary vitamer, best characterised in cow milk, where it is present at single-digit micromolar. Trammell et al. 2016 (J Nutr 146(5):957-963, PMID 27052539, DOI 10.3945/jn.116.230078) found cow milk carries about 12 umol/L of NAD+ precursor vitamins, 60% nicotinamide and 40% NR, and an enzyme-coupled milk assay measured NR at 4.3 +/- 2.6 uM (Ummarino et al. 2017, Food Chem 221:161-168, DOI 10.1016/j.foodchem.2016.10.032). That is about 1.1 mg per litre. Plant foods carry 62 to 1,600 ug per 100 g, highest in wild chicory, banana and orange (Alegre & Pastore 2025, CyTA J Food, DOI 10.1080/19476337.2025.2458753). Every one of these is three orders of magnitude below a 250-1,000 mg capsule. Commercial NR chloride is synthesised, not extracted from milk.

items.dose_gap: Not reachable. At 1.1 mg NR per litre of milk, a 300 mg dose is about 273 litres of milk a day, roughly 1,150 cups; a 1,000 mg dose is about 910 litres. From the richest plant food measured (1.6 mg/100 g) a 300 mg dose is about 19 kg a day. Put the other way, one 250 mg NR capsule contains as much NR as roughly 230 litres of milk. Milk is genuinely the best dietary source of NR and it is still useless as a route to a trial dose.
items.form_caveat: Important. Commercial NR is nicotinamide riboside chloride, a synthesised salt; the free NR in milk is a fragile glycosidic nucleoside that degrades on storage and is reduced in milk from mastitic (S. aureus positive) cows, and Trammell et al. also found conventional milk carried more NR than organic. So even the food number is a moving target. More significant: the whole diet already supplies plenty of the pathway's dominant precursor, nicotinamide, at 15-20 mg/day of niacin equivalents, so NR supplementation is not correcting a dietary gap in NAD+ precursors; it is a pharmacological attempt at a different pharmacokinetic profile. Also note that high-dose nicotinamide-family precursors carry methyl-group and flushing/hepatic considerations at gram level that a glass of milk obviously does not.
items.bioavailability: NR is absorbed orally and raises blood NAD+ in humans, which was the point of the original demonstration (Trammell et al. 2016, Nat Commun 7:12948, DOI 10.1038/ncomms12948). Absorption is not the constraint; the constraint is that food quantities are microgram-scale. There is also a route difference: much oral NR is cleaved to nicotinamide in the gut and liver, so a fraction of any dose acts as plain vitamin B3, which is abundant in food. In milk, NR is free in solution and not bound to milk proteins (NMR testing in Trammell et al. found no binding), so what little is there is available, it is simply trivial in amount.

items.availability_note: This is the one entry on the list where ordinary food beats the supplement outright. Wheat germ, dried soybeans, mushrooms, green peas, fermented soy and some aged cheeses carry milligram-per-portion quantities. Measured mean dietary spermidine intake is 54.7 to 87 umol/day depending on population, that is 7.9 to 12.6 mg/day (Munoz-Esparza et al. 2019, Front Nutr 6:108, PMID 31355206, DOI 10.3389/fnut.2019.00108), and the Bruneck cohort recorded 9 to 11.5 mg/day (Kiechl et al. 2018, Am J Clin Nutr 108(2):371-380, PMID 29955838, DOI 10.1093/ajcn/nqy102). Trial capsules delivered 0.9 mg/day in the SmartAge trial and 1.2 mg/day in the earlier pilot. The diet supplies roughly ten times the capsule.

items.dose_gap: The gap runs backwards, which undercuts the supplement premise. Two tablespoons of wheat germ (14 g) supply 3.1-5.0 mg of spermidine, three to five times the 0.9 mg/day dose used in the 12-month SmartAge trial and still above the 3.3 mg/day used in its follow-up. A quarter-cup of dried soybeans or a cup of sliced mushrooms supplies about 9 mg, close to an entire ordinary day's intake. Measured habitual intakes are 7.9-12.6 mg/day, so a typical 1 mg capsule adds roughly 8-13% on top of what the person is already eating, which is well inside the day-to-day variation of a normal diet. To match a day's dietary spermidine from capsules you would need about ten of them. Anyone who wants more spermidine should buy wheat germ, which costs a fraction of the capsules and delivers several times the dose.
items.form_caveat: Real, in both directions. Most 'spermidine' products are wheat germ extracts standardised to about 1 mg, not purified spermidine, so the label compound is the same molecule as in the food and there is no extraction advantage. Against that, aged cheese and natto also carry biogenic amines (histamine, tyramine, putrescine) which matter for people on MAO inhibitors or with histamine intolerance, so the richest fermented sources are not risk-free foods even though they are ordinary ones. Polyamines are also proliferative signalling molecules and concentrated long-term supplementation lacks the observational safety record that food-level intake has; the epidemiology (Bruneck) supports dietary intake, not high-dose extracts, and cannot be transferred to a capsule. Wheat germ also goes rancid quickly, so buy small and refrigerate.
items.bioavailability: Dietary polyamines are absorbed readily in the upper small intestine, and gut bacteria synthesise more, so intake is not the only input and circulating levels are homeostatically buffered. An exploratory double-blind RCT giving older men 40 mg/day of spermidine, roughly forty times a typical capsule and four times a rich day's diet, reported minimal change in circulating polyamines, which suggests the pharmacokinetic ceiling is reached long before supplement dosing adds anything. Germination changes the picture too: commercially germinated wheat grain measured 19-24 mg/kg spermidine against 221-337 mg/kg for industrially separated wheat germ, an 85% drop, so the processing of the food matters more than any supplement choice.

items.availability_note: Organ meats and oily fish are genuine, substantial sources. Beef heart contains 113 mg/kg, chicken heart 116-132 mg/kg, mackerel dark flesh 43-67 mg/kg (Pravst et al. 2010, Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr 50(4):269-280, DOI 10.1080/10408390902773037, table reproduced in Vaghari et al. 2016, Am J Biochem Biotechnol 12(4):214-219, DOI 10.3844/ajbbsp.2016.214.219). Total habitual dietary intake is 3.8-5.4 mg/day, higher in men than women (Mattila & Kumpulainen 2001, J Food Compost Anal 14:409-417, DOI 10.1006/jfca.2000.0983). So the food is real, and one portion of heart is two to three days of ordinary intake. The problem is that supplement doses are 100-300 mg, which is a different universe. Supplement CoQ10 is produced by microbial fermentation or chemical synthesis, not extracted from beef.

items.dose_gap: Not reachable, though the food is respectable. A 300 mg/day dose requires about 2.7 kg of beef heart, 2.3-2.6 kg of chicken hearts, or 4.7 kg of the very richest sardines, which is about 51 tins a day, rising to over 60 kg if your tins sit at the low end of the measured range. The whole day's ordinary dietary CoQ10 is 3.8-5.4 mg, so a 300 mg capsule is roughly 55 to 80 days of eating compressed into one dose, and even a modest 100 mg capsule is about 20 to 26 days' worth. Anyone whose reason for taking CoQ10 is a claimed pharmacological effect at 100-300 mg cannot get there by eating. Anyone whose reason is simply 'my diet is low in CoQ10' can move the needle meaningfully with a weekly portion of heart, liver or oily fish.
items.form_caveat: Significant. CoQ10 is a large lipophilic quinone (MW 863) and crystalline ubiquinone powder in a dry tablet absorbs very poorly; commercial products use oil suspensions, solubilisates or reduced-form ubiquinol precisely because the raw molecule does not dissolve. Absorption is saturable, so a 300 mg dose does not deliver proportionally more than a 100 mg dose. Food has one genuine advantage here: CoQ10 in meat and fish comes packaged with fat, and taking supplemental CoQ10 with a fatty meal materially improves absorption, so a capsule swallowed on an empty stomach may deliver less than the label implies. Cooking costs some of the food content, with reported losses of roughly 15-32% frying pork cutlets and about 15% grilling beef. Finally, most body CoQ10 is made endogenously and the biosynthetic pathway shares its early steps with cholesterol synthesis, which is the basis of the statin argument; neither food nor supplement changes that pathway.
items.bioavailability: Low and formulation-dependent for the supplement, which is the honest headline. Ubiquinol (reduced) and solubilised formulations achieve higher plasma levels than plain crystalline ubiquinone, and all forms depend on dietary fat and bile for uptake. In the food matrix, CoQ10 sits in mitochondrial membranes and is co-ingested with fat, so uptake per milligram is probably as good or better than a dry capsule, but the milligram totals are 20 to 80 times too small. Note also that the reduced/oxidised split differs between foods: a Japanese survey of 70 food items found ubiquinol-10 above 20 ug/g in pork shoulder, bovine liver, chicken heart, horse mackerel, young yellowtail and soybean oil (Kubo et al. 2008, J Food Compost Anal 21:216-222, DOI 10.1016/j.jfca.2007.09.003), so 'ubiquinol' is not an exclusively supplemental form.

items.availability_note: Alpha-lipoic acid exists in food only as lipoyllysine, covalently attached to lysine residues in the E2 subunits of mitochondrial keto-acid dehydrogenases. Direct LC measurement of meats found 2.11-3.99 ug/g fresh weight in hearts, 0.71-1.40 ug/g in kidney and 0.56-1.17 ug/g in liver (Kaminska & Chwatko 2020, J Agric Food Chem, PMID 32886880, DOI 10.1021/acs.jafc.0c03778), i.e. 0.06-0.40 mg per 100 g. The classic vegetable figures, spinach 3.15 and broccoli 0.94 ug lipoyllysine per gram of DRY weight, work out to about 0.03 and 0.01 mg per 100 g of fresh vegetable. A 600 mg capsule is four to five orders of magnitude above any of these, and the food form is not free lipoic acid at all.

items.dose_gap: Absurd, and worse than the arithmetic suggests. Using the richest food at its richest value (turkey heart, 0.40 mg/100 g), a 600 mg dose is 150 kg of heart per day. Using spinach, the textbook answer, it is about 2,100 kg of raw leaves, roughly 71,000 cups, per day. Broccoli is similar. But the real point is qualitative: what food contains is not alpha-lipoic acid, it is lipoyllysine, lipoic acid amide-bonded to protein-bound lysine. Human lipoamidase activity releases very little free lipoic acid from that bond, so the free-ALA yield from eating spinach is not merely small, it is close to unmeasurable. A 600 mg fasting capsule produces micromolar plasma peaks of free racemic lipoic acid; no quantity of food produces a detectable free-ALA peak at all. This is the clearest food/supplement discontinuity on the list.
items.form_caveat: Large, and it cuts against the supplement. Supplemental ALA is chemically synthesised as a 50:50 racemate of R- and S-lipoic acid; nature makes only the R enantiomer and only protein-bound. So the capsule contains a molecule (S-lipoic acid) that does not exist in food. Absorption also differs by design: capsules are dosed fasting because food reduces ALA absorption by roughly 20-30%, whereas the trace food form is unavoidably taken with food. On safety, the whole food is unremarkable and the concentrated free acid is not: high-dose free ALA has been linked to insulin autoimmune syndrome with severe hypoglycaemia in genetically susceptible people, and there is a paediatric accidental-overdose literature with seizures and death. Spinach has done none of that. If you want the 'antioxidant vegetables' benefit, eat the vegetables; if you want the 600 mg neuropathy dose from the ALADIN/SYDNEY trials, understand you are taking a synthetic drug-dose racemate with its own risk profile, not a vegetable extract.
items.bioavailability: Free supplemental ALA is absorbed reasonably well but cleared very fast, with a plasma half-life on the order of half an hour, and the R enantiomer reaches higher plasma levels than S. Food lipoyllysine is a different question: it is not a bioavailable source of free lipoic acid, because the lipoyl group stays bound to the enzyme protein and is largely digested along with it rather than released as the free dithiol. The measurement literature reflects this, noting that free lipoic acid in tissues is low if present at all and that essentially all of it is protein-bound. Spinach also carries the usual oxalate caveat for other purposes, but oxalate is not the reason spinach fails as a lipoic acid source; the reason is that there is almost none there and what is there is chemically locked up.

items.availability_note: MSM (dimethyl sulfone) really does occur in food, and the numbers are tiny: cow's milk 3.30 mg/kg, coffee 1.60, tomato up to 0.86, alfalfa 0.77, tea 0.30, beer 0.18, Swiss chard up to 0.18, corn up to 0.11 mg/kg (Pearson, Dawson & Lackey 1981, J Agric Food Chem 29(5):1089-1091, DOI 10.1021/jf00107a049; values tabulated in the 2026 MSM review, PMC13071705). Milk, the richest of them, is 0.33 mg per 100 g. Supplement doses are 1.5-6 g/day. The bulk MSM sold as a supplement is not extracted from milk or vegetables: it is manufactured by oxidising dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) with hydrogen peroxide or nitrogen dioxide and then purified by distillation or crystallisation. Functionally this is a synthetic bulk chemical with a token natural presence.

items.dose_gap: One of the widest gaps here. A 3 g/day dose from milk, the richest listed food at 3.30 mg/kg, needs about 909 kg of milk a day, roughly 880 litres or 3,700 cups. From coffee it is about 1,875 litres, some 7,800 mugs. Even the low end of the osteoarthritis trial range, 1.5 g/day, needs 450 kg of milk. Adding up a plausible whole day of milk, coffee, tea, tomatoes and vegetables gives well under 1 milligram of MSM, so a single 3,000 mg dose is thousands of days of dietary MSM at once. There is no food-based route to a supplemental MSM dose, and it should be described as a synthetic sulfur compound taken at pharmacological dose, not as a nutrient you might be short of.
items.form_caveat: Yes, and it is mostly about honesty in marketing. Commercial MSM is made by oxidising DMSO, so it is chemically identical to the trace natural molecule but industrially produced; purity grades differ (distilled versus crystallised) and residual DMSO or solvent is a real quality variable between brands. The common marketing move of pointing at garlic, onions and brassicas as 'natural MSM foods' is wrong: those foods are rich in allicin, thiosulfinates and glucosinolates, which are different sulfur chemistries and not MSM, and eating them does not deliver MSM. Sulfur adequacy in the diet comes from methionine and cysteine in protein, which is a separate question from MSM entirely. There is no case in which a whole food substitutes for an MSM capsule, and equally no evidence that anyone is MSM-deficient.
items.bioavailability: Absorption is not the limiting factor. MSM is a small (94 Da), highly water-soluble, uncharged molecule and is absorbed close to completely after oral dosing, distributing widely including across the blood-brain barrier, which is why it is detectable in cerebrospinal fluid. Circulating MSM in people who take no supplements comes partly from these trace food amounts and partly from bacterial and endogenous metabolism of other sulfur compounds. Because uptake is near-complete for both, the food-versus-supplement comparison reduces entirely to the dose, and the dose ratio is roughly 1:4,000 per cup of milk.

items.availability_note: This is the one supplement on the list whose trial dose is genuinely reachable by eating, because the supplement is simply hydrolysed collagen and several ordinary foods are almost pure collagen. Gelatine is thermally hydrolysed collagen: 85.7 g protein per 100 g with tryptophan recorded as 0.000 g (USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy, Gelatins, dry powder, unsweetened). Plain pork crackling is 61.3 g protein per 100 g with a collagen amino-acid signature (glycine 11.9 g, proline 7.3 g per 100 g). Trial doses are 2.5-15 g/day over 3-18 months (Paul, Leser & Oesser 2019, Nutrients 11(5):1079, PMID 31096622, DOI 10.3390/nu11051079). Bone broth, the popular food answer, is the unreliable one.

items.dose_gap: There is essentially no gap, which is the useful finding. One or two 7 g sachets of ordinary supermarket gelatine (6-12 g of collagen protein) sits squarely inside the 2.5-15 g/day range used in the collagen research, and a 28 g bag of plain pork crackling delivers about as much collagen protein as a 15 g sachet of branded collagen peptides at a fraction of the price. Chicken skin, pork trotters, tendon, oxtail and tinned fish eaten with skin and soft bones all add collagen, though I could not find per-100 g collagen quantifications for those in a citable composition source, so I have not given numbers for them. Bone broth is the one route that does not work reliably: measured amino acid content of broths made to a standardised recipe was significantly lower than a 20 g reference collagen dose for hydroxyproline, glycine and proline, and non-standardised recipes varied enormously, with cafe-prepared broths highest (Alcock, Shaw & Burke 2019, Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 29(3):265-272, PMID 29893587, DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0139). If you want a defined collagen dose from food, use gelatine by weight, not broth.
items.form_caveat: Moderate, and worth stating precisely. Collagen contains no tryptophan at all (USDA records gelatine tryptophan as 0.000 g/100 g), and is low in cysteine, methionine and histidine, so it is an incomplete protein with a PDCAAS effectively at zero and must not be counted as general protein intake; the modelling suggests up to about 36% of total daily protein can be collagen before indispensable amino acid balance suffers (Paul et al. 2019, PMID 31096622). Hydrolysis is a real difference: 'collagen peptides' are enzymatically cut to 2-5 kDa fragments that dissolve in cold liquid and are absorbed partly as di- and tripeptides, whereas gelatine gels and must be dissolved hot, and native collagen in skin and tendon must first be cooked and digested. Whether that changes the outcome is a separate argument, but it is a genuine processing difference rather than marketing. On the food side, pork crackling brings a large load of saturated fat and salt with its collagen, which a sachet of gelatine does not, so 'eat crackling instead of collagen powder' is a real trade-off, not a free win.
items.bioavailability: Genuinely different by form, and here the supplement has a defensible argument. Hydrolysed collagen peptides are absorbed rapidly and hydroxyproline-containing dipeptides such as prolyl-hydroxyproline appear intact in plasma, which is the mechanistic basis of the collagen-peptide literature; a plasma amino acid comparison of dairy and collagen protein confirms the distinctive glycine/proline/hydroxyproline signature of collagen ingestion. Gelatine, being already partly hydrolysed, behaves similarly. Native collagen in skin, tendon and bone requires prolonged moist cooking to become digestible at all, which is exactly why bone broth quantities are unpredictable. Vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation step in endogenous collagen synthesis, so collagen intake without adequate vitamin C is pointless, and eating hydroxyproline does not bypass that requirement.

items.availability_note: There is no meaningful natural food source for either compound, and I will not invent one. Glucosamine hydrochloride is manufactured: chitin-containing raw material, either crustacean shell or the biomass from an Aspergillus niger fermentation, is hydrolysed with food-grade concentrated hydrochloric acid at 100 C, which depolymerises and deacetylates the chitin to glucosamine hydrochloride, then filtered, evaporatively crystallised, centrifuged, washed and flash-dried (EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies, EFSA Journal 2009;1099:1-19, opinion on glucosamine hydrochloride from Aspergillus niger; the opinion states explicitly that the fungal process is the same as the shellfish process except for the raw material). Chondroitin sulfate is extracted from cartilage, commercially mostly frozen bovine trachea, also porcine and shark cartilage. Shellfish shell, fungal mycelium and bovine trachea are not foods in any ordinary diet, neither compound appears in USDA FoodData Central, McCance and Widdowson or any national composition table I could reach, and I found no peer-reviewed per-portion quantification for any ordinary food. Cartilage-containing dishes and bone broth are the nearest food analogue and are not quantifiable: the same problem documented for collagen precursors in bone broth applies (Alcock et al. 2019, PMID 29893587, DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0139), and the one attempt to measure chondroitin sulfate in chicken broths had a limit of quantification of 8 mg per gram of dry material, which is coarse relative to a 1,200 mg daily dose.
items.dose_gap: There is no food quantity, because there is no food source, and the far more interesting number is endogenous. EFSA records human endogenous glucosamine production at 4 to 20 g/day, median about 14 g/day or 230 mg/kg body weight per day for a 60 kg adult (EFSA Journal 2009;1099:1-19). The standard GAIT-trial dose is 1,500 mg glucosamine plus 1,200 mg chondroitin daily, so the supplement adds roughly 10% on top of what the body already makes every day from fructose-6-phosphate and glutamine. That comparison, not a food comparison, is the honest framing: the question is not whether the diet supplies glucosamine (it does not, and does not need to) but whether adding about a tenth again to a large endogenous flux does anything. Prawn and crab shells are chitinous and are the industrial feedstock, but shell is indigestible and is not eaten, so eating prawns delivers no useful glucosamine. Cartilage in a pork knuckle, chicken foot or oxtail does contain glycosaminoglycans, so the intake is not literally zero, but there is no composition data allowing a portion to be quantified and no reason to expect a portion to approach 1.5 g.
items.form_caveat: Several that matter. First, chemical form is not interchangeable in the trial literature: the European positive trials used a specific patented crystalline glucosamine SULFATE, while the large NIH GAIT trial used glucosamine HYDROCHLORIDE, and the results differ, so a shelf product labelled simply 'glucosamine' is not evidence-matched to any particular result. Second, 'vegetarian' or 'shellfish-free' glucosamine from Aspergillus niger fermentation is the same molecule made from fungal chitin rather than shell; it is not a food-derived alternative, it is the same manufactured compound from a different feedstock. Third, shellfish-derived glucosamine is a purified sugar rather than shellfish protein, so it is not the classic tropomyosin allergen route, but labels warn and cautious avoidance is reasonable. Fourth, chondroitin product content notoriously deviates from label claim because it is an extracted polydisperse polysaccharide, and its source is a bovine or shark by-product, which raises both quality-control and sourcing-ethics questions that no food equivalent has. Finally, beware the pet-food and 'joint broth' style reasoning that treats any cartilage-containing dish as therapeutically equivalent to a measured dose; it is not, and nobody has shown it can be.
items.bioavailability: Poor and first-pass-limited for glucosamine: oral glucosamine is largely metabolised on first pass, plasma concentrations reach only low micromolar, far below the millimolar concentrations at which glucosamine affects chondrocytes in cell culture, which is the central pharmacological criticism of the whole category. Absorbed glucosamine is taken into cells by glucose transporters, a process facilitated by insulin, and is phosphorylated to glucosamine-6-phosphate, the same intermediate the body already makes at 4-20 g/day (EFSA Journal 2009;1099:1-19). Chondroitin sulfate is a large sulfated polysaccharide (tens of kDa) and is absorbed mainly after depolymerisation into smaller fragments and constituent sugars, so what reaches the circulation is not the intact molecule that was in the capsule. Any hypothetical food source would face both barriers plus the need to first liberate the glycosaminoglycan from a cooked cartilage matrix, which is why cartilage-rich cooking cannot be treated as a dose.

misclassifications: Glucosamine and chondroitin -> SYNTHETIC is wrong for chondroitin. The submission concedes in its own text that 'Chondroitin sulfate is extracted from cartilage, commercially mostly frozen bovine trachea, also porcine and shark cartilage' - an extract of animal tissue is not a synthetic compound. Edible chicken keel cartilage has been measured at 189 +/- 33 mg chondroitin sulfate per gram (Br Poult Sci 2014), and GAG content has been quantified in chicken feet (J Food Sci 2020) and stewed pig trotters (Foods 2022). Chicken cartilage, chicken feet, pig trotters and shark fin are ordinary foods in Chinese, Japanese and Korean cuisine, and at ~189 mg/g a 6-7 g portion of cartilage would carry a full 1,200 mg dose. Glucosamine alone is legitimately SYNTHETIC (no free glucosamine in food; chitin from shell or Aspergillus biomass is neither digestible nor eaten). The error is bundling two compounds with different availability profiles under one label and then asserting there is 'no food source' for both. Correct handling: split the entry, keep glucosamine SYNTHETIC, classify chondroitin as TRACE-to-RICH-in-niche-foods with the cartilage data cited.

Coenzyme Q10 -> RICH is inconsistent with the submission's own reasoning and partly rests on a mislabelled number. The RICH verdict is applied to a compound whose richest listed food supplies 3.8% of the stated 300 mg dose, while NR is graded TRACE on the strength of milk being 'genuinely the best dietary source' - the same structure of argument, opposite label. The submission's own dose_gap concludes 'not reachable'. Two of the four organ-meat figures that make CoQ10 look rich are also compromised: chicken heart's 116.2-132.2 mg/kg is actually chicken liver, and pork heart (118.1-282 mg/kg, the richest food source of all) is missing entirely. A MODERATE / PARTIAL grade is defensible (a 100 g portion of heart really is 2-3 days of ordinary intake), RICH in the same scheme that gives spermidine and collagen RICH is not, because for those two the food genuinely reaches or exceeds the trial dose.

MSM -> TRACE reaches the right label on void evidence. Every number in the entry traces to Pearson, Dawson & Lackey 1981, which measured dimethyl SULFOXIDE (DMSO), not dimethyl sulfone (MSM). The classification survives (nobody claims milk delivers grams of MSM), but the availability_note's confident 'MSM really does occur in food, and the numbers are tiny: cow's milk 3.30 mg/kg...' asserts a compositional fact the cited literature does not establish. The correct classification is TRACE / UNQUANTIFIED, with an explicit note that the widely circulated MSM food table is a mislabelled DMSO table.

NMN -> TRACE is the right label but the supporting note is self-contradicting. 'Sub-milligram-per-100 g levels, roughly 100 to 1,000 times below a single capsule' is refuted two sentences later by the submission's own citation of Alegre & Pastore 2025 at up to 13,000 ug/100 g (13 mg/100 g), which is ~19x below a 250 mg capsule per 100 g portion, not 100-1,000x, and is not sub-milligram. TRACE still holds against a 250-1,000 mg dose; the quantitative framing does not.

Correctly classified, challenged and upheld: Nicotinamide riboside TRACE (milk at 1.1-1.3 mg/L and plant foods at 62-1,600 ug/100 g are three orders below a capsule - confirmed); Alpha-lipoic acid TRACE (confirmed, and the qualitative point that food contains protein-bound lipoyllysine rather than free racemic ALA is the strongest single observation in the submission); Spermidine RICH (confirmed - habitual intake 7.9-15.0 mg/day genuinely exceeds the 0.9 mg trial capsule by ~10x); Collagen peptides RICH (confirmed - a 7 g gelatine sachet at 85.6% protein sits inside the 2.5-15 g/day trial range).

verification_report.net_assessment:
Unusually strong submission by the standards of this genre, and the arithmetic is the best part of it: I recomputed roughly sixty unit conversions, per-portion figures and percent-of-dose calculations and the overwhelming majority are correct to the stated precision, including every nmol/g-to-mg/100 g polyamine conversion, the NR micromolar-to-mg/L step, the spinach and broccoli dry-to-fresh water-content conversions, the sardine-tin and cucumber counts, and all seven Mills NMN food ranges (which match Table 1 of the source exactly). Nine of eleven cited PMIDs and every checkable DOI resolve to the paper claimed. The qualitative reasoning on lipoyllysine versus free racemic ALA, on gelatine as a defined collagen dose versus bone broth, and on endogenous glucosamine flux versus supplement dose is genuinely good and better sourced than most published consumer material.

Five defects are serious enough to require correction before publication. First, the entire MSM food table is DMSO data: Pearson, Dawson & Lackey 1981 is titled 'Naturally occurring levels of dimethyl sulfoxide...' and the 2026 review the submission leans on silently relabels those eight numbers as MSM. Second, CoQ10 'chicken hearts 116.2-132.2 mg/kg' is chicken liver; chicken heart is 92.3-192 mg/kg, and the Pravst-derived table contains no chicken heart row at all. Third, the NR bioavailability claim that Trammell's NMR 'found no binding' inverts the source, which reports positive WaterLOGSY signals consistent with protein binding. Fourth, the spermidine pharmacokinetic argument misstates Senekowitsch 2023 as 40 mg/day in older men with minimal polyamine change, when it was 15 mg/day in 12 healthy volunteers with a significant rise in plasma spermine. Fifth, chondroitin is filed as SYNTHETIC despite the entry itself describing it as a cartilage extract, and despite published quantification of ~189 mg chondroitin sulfate per gram of edible chicken keel cartilage.

Three further problems are citation hygiene rather than substance: the Kubo 2008 DOI resolves to an unrelated acrylamide paper (correct is 10.1016/j.jfca.2007.10.003, pages 199-210); the EFSA 4-20 g/day endogenous glucosamine figure belongs to the 2013 ANS opinion, not the 2009 Aspergillus niger opinion; and the milk NR value of 4.3 +/- 2.6 uM is Trammell's, not Ummarino's. Two per-food figures are quietly optimistic where a range exists (mushroom and soybean spermidine), one omission materially weakens a headline claim (pork heart is the richest CoQ10 food and is absent), and the NMN entry contradicts itself by citing a 13 mg/100 g source while asserting sub-milligram content and computing a 22-100 kg broccoli gap. The eight USDA FDC IDs could not be checked this session because the FDC API rate-limited DEMO_KEY, so they are marked unverified rather than confirmed. Verdict: publishable after the five substantive fixes and the three citation repairs; the classification scheme also needs stating explicitly, because as applied it grades CoQ10 RICH and NR TRACE on materially the same evidence.
